newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Analyst comment on Hoogovens yr results.
newsitem.headline: Analyst comment on Hoogovens yr results.

text.p: Steel and aluminium group Hoogovens NV on Thursday reported 1996 net profit of 326 million guilders, well below 1995's 507 million but above analysts' forecasts of 260-310 million guilders.

"It is better than expected. They have realised 326 million (guilders) and that, in my opinion, is a formidable result compared with other steel makers. They also foresee a higher result in 1997 and that's positive."
"The 100 guilders (share price) level doesn't seem too far away and I think we keep our buy recommendation," he added.

"It's a very good result. The indication at the half year point was for a bit lower. The second half showed some recovery, notably in steel prices. They're stable now, but they're up from August 1996.

"The future for Hoogovens looks good, the economy is improving, steel prices are good and financially the company is very sound. We have had it as a buy since last December and certainly if these figures hold out we'll be very satisfied."

"This looks good. Both in steel and aluminium, results were above our expectations, while turnover was also more than we counted on. Hoogovens' statement over 1997, its unchanged dividend and the fact they said they would raise investments, show the company has confidence in its future and the cash-flow it will generate.
"I think the strong pound and dollar lay a base for somewhat higher steel prices in the second quarter of this year. And Hoogovens' capacity use will be further increased.
"All in all, my first impression is positive."

"It is higher than I expected for the second half, but it seems mainly due to the lower tax rate (compared with the first half). Apart from that, there are no real surprises. The statement with regard to '97 is positive, but it's not very surprising either. That's expected as steel prices increased in the fourth quarter of last year and the volume development (in the industry) is expected to be more than five percent in '97. The first half of this year will clearly be higher than the first half of 1996."
